snippet.title: How We Retired Early With $540K At 40 In Colorado
snippet.description:
In 2012, Debbie Emick received a series of troubling diagnoses, forcing her to retire from teaching two years later. She and her husband, Chris, then set out on a path of achieving FIRE — financial independence, retire early. An initial investment of $60,000 grew and they bought 17 rental properties from 2016 to 2019. That income stream allowed Chris to retire from his IT job in November 2019 after they accumulated $540,000 in savings and retirement accounts and $1.1 million in real estate.

snippet.title: The Main Problem with the “FIRE” Movement
snippet.description:
The FIRE movement (Financial Independence, Retire Early) focuses heavily on the math—but many people overlook the psychological blind spots, hidden risks, and real-life challenges that don’t show up in a spreadsheet. In this video, we break down the biggest downsides of FIRE, including early retirement risks, financial independence mistakes, and why financial freedom doesn’t always lead to happiness.

In this video, we discuss:

Why early retirement doesn’t always lead to happiness
Hidden risks and blind spots most people ignore
Safe Withdrawal Rates in Retirement
The trade-off between financial freedom and life purpose

How to think about financial independence more realistically

snippet.title: What I've Done Since Discovering the FIRE Movement | Four Years Later
snippet.description:
Today's video is really looking back at the last five years and the different life milestones that were achieved. I've mentioned in the past that my money journey started in May 2017, the same is true of my FIRE journey. 

I came across the financial independence / retire early while on my long commutes to and from work. In 2017, my main focus was debt pay-off then in 2018, it shifted to saving for an emergency fund and to move out of my parents' basement. In 2019, we moved out and the reality of paying for rent hit me, this was also the year I finally asked for the promotion I wanted. Then in 2020, we were suddenly working from home 24/7 and on lockdown so we made the decision to move back to the suburbs and into the basement at Ari's mom's. With this move, I was able to increase my savings rate.

I'll be following this video up with a Net Worth through the years look at where and how my money was growing.

snippet.title: OUR JOURNEY TO FINANCIAL FREEDOM AT 38 | The FIRE Movement
snippet.description:
9 years ago, we had a vision of becoming millionaires and achieving financial freedom!  We wanted a life that focused on spending quality time with each other, our children, family and friends.  We planned to achieve financial independence and join the fire movement by retiring young!

In this video, we walk through how we became millionaires at age 35 and chose early retirement at age 38 (like CNBC Make It).  We made short term sacrifices to have a lifetime of freedom with our three young children.

We talk about our backgrounds and share the story of how we met.  Our desire for fire retirement started for each of us when we were young and grew stronger when we started having children 5 years ago! 

One of our main objectives for creating Holy City Family is to teach our children, and the next generation how to budget, save money, and invest it wisely. Our children are still a bit young (3 under 5), but we have plans to incorporate financial education into their homeschool curriculum and every day lives. Although both of us both have college degrees and had high GPAs, we surprisingly learned very little about financial literacy during our academic years.

As we share our FIRE journey with you, we hope that you feel inspired and see that IF we can do this, anyone can.  We didn't have a 6 figure income and we have 3 young children under the age of 5.

People think you have to have at least a six figure income to reach FIRE, but that was NOT the case for us. Once Jerad and I got the idea in our head to reach financial independence, we wanted to do everything we could to reach our goal as soon as possible.

In addition to our budgeting, saving and investments in the stock market, we slow flipped the houses we were living in for a profit.  In our last 3 houses in the Charlotte area,  we made over $150,000 in profit. By ‘slow flipping’ we mean that it wasn’t your traditional house flipping strategy, we renovated the houses we lived in ourselves and we did it over the course of a couple years on average.

Once the wheels started turning… we were saving up to 70% of our income and investing it.  It’s been amazing to watch our savings and investments grow over the years.  It really encouraged us and showed as that achieving FIRE could actually happen!

To us FIRE means, “Running to something” and not from something. Being able to spend more time with each other and the kids. Being fully present and experiencing our children growing up. We want to leave a legacy for our children and future generations. Want people to know there is another path to a more fulfilling life.

The FIRE (Financial Independence, Retire Early) movement has evolved significantly over the past few years. Once considered viable for people with modest incomes, it’s now seen by many as out of reach, especially in a post 2020 economy marked by surging costs, inflated housing prices, and a more precarious job market. But FIRE isn’t dea,d it just looks different now. What once worked in a low-cost, stable environment needs to be re-evaluated and adapted to reflect today’s economic reality.

The script explores four core tiers of FIRE LeanFIRE, Standard FIRE, ChubbyFIRE, and FatFIRE, each reflecting varying lifestyles and financial goals. It also highlights newer, more flexible offshoots like CoastFIRE (where you front-load investing early and coast later), BaristaFIRE (combining part time work with partial withdrawals), and Flexible FIRE (blending part-time work and income streams with modest withdrawals). These evolving paths offer a way to pursue financial freedom without relying on the rigid extremes of traditional FIRE models.

In today’s environment, building a FIRE plan means focusing on adaptability and intentional strategy. That includes increasing your income through methods like the "Up, Out, In" approach, moving up in your current company, finding better opportunities elsewhere, and reskilling to stay ahead of job market shifts, especially with AI reshaping the workforce. Managing spending, tracking every dollar, and pre-saving for future expenses like medical bills, car replacements, and home maintenance are more important than ever to stay on track.

Additionally, geographic arbitrage, moving to lower-cost areas to stretch income and savings, can help reduce the time it takes to reach financial independence. The key message is that the core of FIRE is still achievable, but it requires a modern mindset. That means letting go of outdated formulas, taking ownership of what you can control, and building a lifestyle and financial plan that reflects today’s challenges and opportunities.

The FIRE Movement - Financial Independence Retire Early Explained

FIRE is an acronym of Financial Independence and Retiring Early. It is a movement that is growing around the world, based on a very aggressive saving and investing strategy, people can get to a point where they are effectively retired at a very young age. Why? We need to consider the fact that as the world is changing, people are changing too, and so their needs and what they want in life. Let's find out more in this video.

snippet.title: The FIRE Movement: A Beginner’s Guide | How I’m Retiring at 30
